Thank you for submitting your article "The landscape of regulatory genes in brain-wide neuronal phenotypes of a vertebrate brain" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Koichi Kawakami as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Didier Stainier as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

The reviewers recognized the authors performed enormous amounts of works and the data presented in the manuscript should be useful resources for neurobiologists. However the reviewers indicated the following major concerns which should be addressed by the authors.

1) The validity of clustering. The reviewers think the authors need control analysis for this.

2) For "divergent" and "convergent" classes, the hypothesis presented by the authors were not proven. To experimentally prove this is a bit too much for the present paper. Instead, the reviewers request more statistical data to support these ideas.

Reviewer #1:

In this manuscript, the authors performed single cell RNA-seq analysis of ~46,000 cells from the zebrafish larval brain and identified 68 clusters and mapped them on the brain regions. They found (1) region-specific markers, (2) correlation with cell types in juvenile fish, (3) 1099 effector genes out of 1402 genes used to define the clusters, (4) and 48 neuronal clusters and 20 non-neurons including glia. Then, they analyzed scRNA-seq using vmat (monoaminergic) and vachte (cholinergic) transgenic fish and (5) identified 22 and 14 neuromodulator clusters. (6) The neuromodulator clusters were further analyzed for neurotransmitter types and they revealed coexpression patterns.

In the hierarchical classification, they identified (7) 11 "sister clusters" that have similar expression profiles for effector genes, that had the same neurotransmitter types but did not show brain region preference. Then they examined TF profiles in neurotransmitter type neurons and identified 14 TF sister clusters. They found (8) one effector gene cluster that match with a TF cluster (matched) and 10 effector gene clusters that did not match with TF clusters (convergent) (these expressed the same neurotransmitters), and also found (9) neuromodulator clusters were well matched with TF profiles (matched). (10) They found the same TF clusters can express different effector genes also (divergent).

Then they aimed to see relationship between TF and morphology. They sorted tectal glut cells and identified 11 TF clusters. Then they made Bac-gal4 for 15 TFs and performed intersection using Cre-glut. (11) They analyzed 574 tectal neurons and found that TF could mark multiple morphology.

Since (in the divergent class) TF did not correlate with effector, they analyzed RNA binding proteins. (12) RNA-binding proteins were expressed differently in different neuron clusters.

Strength: The authors performed a comprehensive analysis of brain cells by single-cell RNA-seq. The scRNA-seq data presented here will be a good reference when the neuroscientists study a certain neuronal types, for instance searching for marker genes expressed in the neuronal clusters of their interest. Also, the amount of work is enormous.

Weakness: The contents of this paper are rather descriptive and poor in mechanistic aspects (causal relationship). Also I felt difficulty in following the manuscript since experiments were not described as hypothesis-driven.

1) The authors prepared cells for sc-RNA seq in different ways and this made the manuscript a bit confusing. Please clarify the purpose and reason for the to do so.

2) I think only "positive" data is the identification of the "matched" class. For "convergent" and "divergent" classes, many other explanations will be possible since there are no mechanistic analysis. For "convergent" class, examine if any TFs with weak expression had been overlooked. For "divergent" class, examine if the authors can find specific (classes) of RBP as real candidates.

3) As for the section describing the morphology, 11 clusters identified, and the 7 morphological classes seemed irrelevant. Also, relationship between 6TFs and the 7 morphological classes did not sound although the work for construction of 15 BACs should have to be enormous. Rewrite the section for readers to be understandable.

Reviewer #2:

In this study, the authors investigated how diverse neuronal types develop in the brain by using single-cell RNA sequencing methods.

The authors performed rigorous data collections for different brain regions, monoaminergic neurons, catecholaminergic neurons, and glutamatergic neurons. Such careful data collection for different types of neurons and brain regions has not been done for larval zebrafish. Their data will be a valuable resource for the neuroscience field.

They further found that the expression patterns of transcription factors are not necessarily predictive of the expression patterns effector genes that constitute the "terminal features" of neuronal cell types. Such predictiveness depends on the cell types. In neuromodulatory neurons, TF expression is predictive of effector gene expressions. On the contrary, in "neurotransmitter" neurons, which represent glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, this relationship is loose and diverse. This finding, if confirmed, will advance our understanding of how diverse neuronal types develop in vertebrate brains.

The major weakness of this study is the lack of statistical controls in their analyses. I raise two examples here. First, the classification of "convergent types" and "divergent types" is solely based on hierarchical clustering analysis and its distance measures which are not validated by sub-sampling or by other statistical methods. Therefore, this analysis cannot rule out the possibility that such classification arises from large variations of gene expressions within the analyzed populations and that there are no such distinct populations.

The second example is their analysis of the expression of RNA-binding proteins. They show that the RBPs have differential expression in "divergent" cluster pairs. However, they do not show whether such differential expression is more prevalent among "divergent" cluster pairs than in other neuronal cluster pairs. If this is not the case, the differential expression of RBPs may not be the reason for the differential expression of effector genes.

Although the claim of this paper may be of broad interest in the neuroscience field, the above weaknesses significantly affect the reliability of the conclusion of this paper. Therefore, I recommend a revision of this manuscript for its publication in eLife.

1) The classification of "convergent" and "divergent" types in Figure 3 needs quantitative validation to exclude the possibility that such classification arises from large variations of gene expressions. This problem is unavoidable for analyses that solely rely on hierarchical clustering methods and their distance measures. Showing expression patterns of several example genes does not reinforce the conclusion, as it is always possible to find genes that show differential expression between any given cluster pairs. The result of neuromodulatory neurons only works as a partial control, as they are different neuronal types. This study needs to reinforce the validity of the classification by cross-validation of cluster distances among samples or by using unbiased statistical methods other than clustering.

2) The analysis of differential expression of RNA-binding proteins among "divergent" neuronal clusters needs statistical control. The authors need to show that RBPs in "divergent" pairs have more divergent expression patterns than in "convergent" pairs in an unbiased, quantitative way. Again, showing the example of few genes is not enough. Otherwise, RBPs cannot explain the divergence of effector gene expression from similar TF expression profiles.

3) The coloring schemes in figures are confusing. For example, I can see many color schemes in Figure 1. We only need two types of classification: (1) brain regions and (2) cell types. Figure 1a may not need colors/numberings and only need names for some of the clusters. Also, the classification presented in Figure 1c (Glu-GABA-P-R) and the one presented in Figure 1g (I- II, III, IV, V) are redundant. I understand that these different schemes serve different purposes, but I recommend unifying these classification schemes for clarity. This unification may need reordering of figure panels.

Reviewer #3:

In this manuscript, the authors performed single-cell RNA sequencing of >60,000 cells across the whole zebrafish brain with region- and molecular- identity. Using the acquired transcriptomes, the authors tried to deduce the regulation logic of neuronal diversification by comparing sister clusters in hierarchical clustering based on effector genes and regulatory TFs. The author showed that while TF similarity in modulatory neurons largely predict the similarity of their neuromodulator types, neurotransmitter types and their TF profiles usually do not agree. Further analysis of cell-type divergence from common TF regulators revealed an interesting differential enrichment of RNA binding proteins, which are potentially involved in post-transcriptional regulation of neuronal identity.

The transcriptomic data is comprehensive and of high quality, with cells covering the entire zebrafish brain, and with close-up analysis generated by new experiments to give higher discriminatory power. The data offers a valuable resource to the developmental neurobiology community. Some patterns (e.g. phenotypic convergence) echoes the findings in invertebrate nervous systems. Difference in regulatory logic of neurotransmitter vs. neuromodulator types, as well as the identification of post-transcriptional regulator genes are novel and interesting.

However, some caveats in data analysis may affect the reliability of the conclusions. The key claims in the study heavily relied on analysis of "sister clusters", i.e. clusters of cells with most similar TF or effector gene profiles. Yet not enough justification was given to the selection of such clusters or the focus only on the direct sibling clusters, and the fact that neurotransmitter and neuromodulator data were acquired differently adds complication to the interpretation of the result. Meanwhile, although the descriptive data in this study gives a detailed account of neuronal diversity, the lack of causal evidence and/or concrete mechanistic explanation between regulatory genes and terminal effectors rendered the conclusions a bit elusive -they tend to fell into providing interesting insight while failing to account for alternative explanations.

Overall, I think the claims are supported by the data for the most part, and with the addition of certain control and additional analyses, it enhances our understanding of vertebrate neuronal diversification as a thought-provoking descriptive study: Genes involved in convergent or divergent cell types identified in this study serve as curious candidate for follow-up investigation. Regulatory logic and mechanisms, when compared with similar studies in invertebrates, can help us to gain insights on the origin and evolution of the nervous system.

1. In the first and second section of Result, clusters of the transcriptome data were treated as the "smallest unit" for subsequent analysis. However, there's a lack of justification for the clustering criteria: i.e. how distinct the clusters are, and how robust the subsequent analysis result is if cell-type clustering is performed slightly differently. This is especially problematic because even the authors themselves have shown that given cleaner quality data (e.g. modulatory neurons in FAC sorted cells vs. whole brain), clustering partition could be different. Additional control analysis would be necessary to show clustering makes sense and robust to noise level in the data.

2. The authors compared the 8dpf brain transcriptomes with juvenile brain in Raj et al., 2018 and claimed that "are likely to represent the full cellular diversity of the mature zebrafish brain". The stretch is a bit far because they partitioned the data only using variable genes expressed in both datasets, i.e. differentially expressed genes involved in subsequent diversification were not accounted for. I think at best this analysis serves as a similarity claim rather than "full" cellular diversity.

3. Result Section 3: a major weakness in the design of analysis is the focus only on "sister clusters", which can be sensitive to your cluster partition and does not necessarily represent the real diversification event. To compare the landscape of TF and effector gene expression, there are many alternative methods accounting for the full spectrum of cell types rather than just the most similar sibling clusters. I would suggest two supplementary analyses: (1) A population-level statistical analysis to show the difference in regulatory logic across all cell types regardless of clustering, even in the less similar cells. (2) A test to ensure that the disagreement between TF and effectors does not disappear as we break clusters in neurotransmitter types into smaller sub types. As stated in point #1, it is necessary for the authors to demonstrate the difference in regulatory logic between transmitter and modulator types is not a result of different noise level in the data.

4. Result Section 4: the criteria for assigning TF expression to morphology class is again relying too much on binary classification. In particular, the authors considered a TF to be a marker for the morphology class "appeared for at least 4 times". The morphology classes are very different in sizes and this is an unfair comparison. Rather more quantitative metrics and vigorous statistical tests should be used to support this conclusion.

5. Result Section 5: in addition to transcriptome data, it would be nice if the authors can demonstrate some causal links between the RBP genes and the cell type regulation, or verify experimentally that they indeed encode neurons with different identity, morphology or functions. If additional experiments to demonstrate causal links are not possible, the authors should sufficiently account for alternative explanations for cell type divergence. Besides post-transcriptional regulation, there are a lot of other factors that could affect gene diversification, including early regulators that are transiently expressed in the embryo that primed fate selection, and external signaling factors in the neuron's environment. Such information was lost as only mature neurons are sequenced with very little spatial context.

In the revised manuscript, the authors mainly added three additional control analyses that increased the credibility of the conclusion, including:

1) Robustness analysis of the clustering result using Jaccard similarity of subsampled data.

2) Analysis of the matched/convergent/divergent patterns of the glutamatergic/GABAergic neurons based on relaxed criteria that include not only the terminal sister clusters, but also non-sibling clusters with relatively close relationships.

claims.evidence: The manuscript identifies 10 pairs of glutamatergic/GABAergic clusters that exhibited similar TF profiles but different effector gene profiles (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).

claims.claim: A library of RNA-binding proteins differentially marked divergent pair clusters.
claims.source: It led us to identify a library of RNA-binding proteins that differentially marked divergent pair clusters, suggesting the post-transcriptional regulation of neuron diversification.
claims.evidence: GO analysis of differentially expressed genes between divergent sister clusters revealed that many genes encoded RBPs (Figure 5A), and the manuscript provides a comprehensive list of these RBPs (Figure 5—source data 1).

claims.claim: The larval zebrafish brain comprises approximately 100,000 cells.
claims.source: The larval zebrafish brain comprises only about 100,000 cells, thus providing an outstanding vertebrate model for studying cell diversity within the entire brain, using single-cell transcriptome analysis with full cell coverage by the 10× Genomics Platform.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about zebrafish brain cell numbers.

claims.claim: The study obtained transcriptomes of 65,253 cells and selected 45,746 cells for further analysis after filtering.
claims.source: We obtained the transcriptomes of 65,253 cells and selected 45,746 cells for further analysis after filtering out low-quality data (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is directly stated in the results section describing the data processing pipeline.

claims.claim: All cells were aggregated into 68 clusters using high-variance genes (n = 1402).
claims.source: Then aggregated all cells into 68 clusters using high-variance genes (n = 1402) in t-SNE plot (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A displaying the t-SNE plot with 68 numbered clusters.

claims.claim: Most clusters had a high Jaccard index greater than 0.6, indicating robustness.
claims.source: The Jaccard index-based analysis showed that most clusters had a high Jaccard index greater than 0.6, indicating the robustness of these clusters (details in Materials and methods) (Tang et al., 2020) except for a few neuronal clusters from sub-OT (Clusters 52, 66), and non-neuronal clusters (neuroprogenitors: Clusters 37, 56; radial astrocytes: 65, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes using the Jaccard index to evaluate cluster stability, with results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and cites the method from Tang et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Foxg1a, en2a, and hoxb3a were explicitly expressed in all cell types of the forebrain, optic tectum, and hindbrain, respectively.
claims.source: For instance, foxg1a, en2a, and hoxb3a were explicitly expressed in all cell types of the Fore, OT, and Hind, respectively (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D as a dot plot displaying expression levels of region-specific marker genes.

claims.claim: Brain region-specific genes exhibited a conserved region-specific expression pattern in the mouse brain.
claims.source: Interestingly, these brain region-specific genes also exhibited a conserved region-specific expression pattern in the mouse brain (Hanks et al., 1995, Manzanares et al., 2001, Kumamoto and Hanashima, 2017).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites three references (Hanks et al., 1995, Manzanares et al., 2001, Kumamoto and Hanashima, 2017) to support the conservation of region-specific gene expression patterns across species.

claims.claim: The ratio of glutamatergic to GABAergic neurons was highest in the forebrain and lowest in the hindbrain.
claims.source: The ratio of glutamatergic to GABAergic neurons was the highest in the forebrain and lowest in the hindbrain, indicating that glutamatergic neurons predominantly belonged to the forebrain, whereas glycinergic neurons mainly resided in the hindbrain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pie charts in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D showing the compositions of different neuron types in brain regions.

claims.claim: The 68 clusters exhibited high overlap with their counterparts in the juvenile zebrafish brain.
claims.source: Moreover, the Lawson-Hanson algorithm for non-negative least squares (NNLS) analysis using cluster-specific marker genes (top 20, Figure 1—source data 4) showed that these 68 clusters exhibited a high overlap with their counterparts in the juvenile zebrafish brain recently reported (Raj et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes using NNLS analysis to compare their data with previously published juvenile zebrafish data (Raj et al., 2018), with results shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The brain at 8 dpf mostly represented cellular diversity in the juvenile brain.
claims.source: Thus, our analysis indicated that the brain at 8 dpf mostly represented cellular diversity in the juvenile brain.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the NNLS analysis showing high correlation between 8 dpf and juvenile zebrafish brain cell clusters.

claims.claim: The majority of variable genes (78.4%, n = 1099) were effector genes.
claims.source: Furthermore, Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of 1402 variable genes used for the classification of all 68 clusters showed that the majority of these genes (78.4%, n = 1099) were effector genes, which could be classified as neuropeptides, receptors, transporters, ion channels, synaptic proteins, and cell adhesion molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by GO analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claims.claim: All 68 clusters were first segregated into two groups: neuronal cells (48 clusters, 37,880 cells) and non-neuronal cells (20 clusters, 7866 cells).
claims.source: All 68 clusters were first segregated into two groups, neuronal cells (48 clusters, 37,880 cells) and non-neuronal cells (20 clusters, 7866 cells) (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the hierarchical dendrogram in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Branch IIa included 22 subclasses of excitatory glutamatergic neurons.
claims.source: Branch IIa included 22 subclasses of excitatory glutamatergic neurons (vgluta2a+-gad1b--glyt2-), whereas Branch IIb inhibitory neurons included 17 subclasses of GABAergic neurons (vgluta2a-/gad1b+) and 1 subclass of glycinergic neurons (vgluta2a--gad1b+-glyt2+, Cluster17, Figure 1—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text describing the hierarchical classification of neuronal cells based on neurotransmitter markers.

claims.claim: Using Tg (ETvmat2:GFP) transgenic fish, the study could examine transcriptomes of DA neurons, 5-HT neurons, and NE neurons.
claims.source: Using this fishline, we could examine transcriptomes of DA neurons, 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) neurons, and norepinephrinergic (NE) neurons (Wen et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and cites Wen et al., 2008 as the source for the transgenic line characterization.

claims.claim: A total of 5368 vmat2-expressing cells were obtained and aggregated into 22 clusters.
claims.source: After the filtering procedures described above, we obtained a total of 5368 vmat2-expressing cells (Materials and methods). The analysis aggregated these cells into 22 clusters in t-SNE plots (Figure 2B), more than those found using whole-brain samples (two DA, one 5-HT, and three ChAT; Figure 1—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B displaying the t-SNE plot with 22 numbered clusters.

claims.claim: The majority of clusters (20/22) were stable using mean/median Jaccard index >0.6 as cutoff.
claims.source: To further validate the stability of clusters, we used the Jaccard index, which showed that the majority of clusters (20/22) were stable using mean/median Jaccard index >0.6 as cutoff (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the JaccardRainCloudPlot in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The majority of 5-HT (8/14) and DA clusters (5/7) expressed GABAergic markers gad1b/gad2.
claims.source: Further examination of these neuromodulator clusters for their expression of specific neurotransmitters showed that the majority of 5-HT (8/14) and DA clusters (5/7) expressed GABAergic markers gad1b/gad2 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the dot plot in Figure 2C displaying expression of neurotransmitter markers.

claims.claim: TF-based and effector gene-based trees were distinct in terms of matching node and tree distances (tree distance = 0.71).
claims.source: Notably, TF-based and effector gene-based trees were distinct in terms of matching node (only one matching node: Clusters 9/61) and tree distances (tree distance = 0.71, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the effector gene-based sister clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) might express different TF profiles.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the tree comparison analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Out of 11 effector genes-based sister clusters, only one pair could be found in TF-based sister clusters (Clusters 9/61, 'matched pattern').
claims.source: We found out of 11 effector genes-based sister clusters, only one pairs could be found in TF-based sister clusters (Clusters 9/61, 'matched pattern', Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Ten effector gene-based sister clusters were separated in TF-based classification, suggesting neurons with similar terminal features mostly expressed different TF profiles ('convergent pattern').
claims.source: And other 10 effector gene-based sister clusters were separated in TF-based classification, suggesting that neurons with similar terminal features mostly expressed different TF profiles ('convergent pattern'; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The population-level analysis identified 19 pairs of effector gene-based similar pair clusters, 5 with matched pattern and 14 with convergent pattern.
claims.source: The population-level analysis identified 19 pairs of effector gene-based similar pair clusters, 5 with matched pattern and 14 with convergent pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by scatter plots and tables in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-G.

claims.claim: By intersecting hierarchical sister cluster analysis and population-level statistical analysis, eight pairs of effector gene-based glutamatergic/GABAergic similar pair clusters were identified, one with matched pattern and seven with convergent pattern.
claims.source: To overcome this discrepancy, we intersected the results from hierarchical sister cluster analysis and population-level statistical analysis, and identified eight pairs of effector gene-based glutamatergic/GABAergic similar pair clusters, one with matched pattern and seven with convergent pattern (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Tectal glutamatergic Cluster 1 and hindbrain glutamatergic Cluster 31 shared effector gene profiles but differentially expressed TF profiles.
claims.source: The first case was a glutamatergic pair cluster from different brain regions: tectal glutamatergic Cluster 1 and hindbrain glutamatergic Cluster 31 shared effector gene profiles including camk2n1a/stmn4/cbln2b/olfm3a/cd63, but differentially expressed TF profiles, atf5b/bhlhe41/lhx1a and ddit3/cebpb/lef1, respectively (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as an example of convergent pattern and shown in violin plots in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: GABAergic clusters in the forebrain (Cluster 36) and the sub-OT (Cluster 16) shared effector gene profiles but differentially expressed TF profiles.
claims.source: The second case was GABAergic pair cluster from different brain regions: GABAergic clusters in the forebrain (Cluster 36) and the sub-OT (Cluster 16) shared effector gene profiles mcl1a/cbln1/tspan18a/dusp5/ncaldb, but differentially expressed TF profiles, tbr1b/foxg1a/barhl2 and otpa/otpb/six6a, respectively (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as an example of convergent pattern and shown in violin plots in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Using hierarchical sister cluster analysis, 5/8 of neuromodulator-type sister clusters matched with those defined by TF profiles ('matched pattern'), 3/8 sister clusters were found to be separated in TF-based classification ('convergent pattern').
claims.source: Using hierarchical sister cluster analysis, 5/8 of neuromodulator-type sister clusters matched with those defined by TF profiles ('matched pattern'), 3/8 sister cluster were found to be separated in TF-based classification ('convergent pattern', Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-G.

claims.claim: Population-level statistical analysis found eight pairs with matched pattern and one pair with convergent pattern for neuromodulator neurons.
claims.source: Then, we also performed the population-level statistical analysis using all genes or 80% genes (subsampling) to compare the landscape of TF and effector gene expression. We found eight pairs with matched pattern and one pair with convergent pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H-I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3H-I.

claims.claim: By intersecting hierarchical sister cluster analysis and population-level statistical analysis, six pairs of similar neuromodulator pair clusters were identified, five with matched pattern, and one with convergent pattern.
claims.source: Thus, we intersected hierarchical sister cluster analysis and population-level statistical analysis, and identified six pairs of similar neuromodulator pair clusters, five with matched pattern, and one with convergent pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 3J-L).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3J-L.

claims.claim: Neuromodulator pairs with similar effector gene profiles predominantly were 'matched' pattern, whereas neurotransmitter pairs with similar effector gene profiles mainly were 'convergent' pattern.
claims.source: Together with the above results of neuromodulator-type and neurotransmitter types, our analysis showed that neuromodulator pairs with similar effector gene profiles predominantly were 'matched' pattern, whereas neurotransmitter pairs with similar effector gene profiles mainly were 'convergent' pattern (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the bar plot in Figure 3E comparing the proportions of different patterns.

claims.claim: The distance between TF-based and effector-based hierarchical tree of neuromodulator neurons (Tree distance = 0.38) was lower than that of glutamatergic/GABAergic neurons (tree distance = 0.71).
claims.source: Moreover, we performed global tree measurement using the R package 'TreeDist', and found that the distance between TF-based and effector-based hierarchical tree of neuromodulator neurons (Tree distance = 0.38, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B) was lower than that of glutamatergic/GABAergic neurons (tree distance = 0.71, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting distinct TF regulatory logic of effector-based phenotypes between neurotransmitter-type and neuromodulator-type at the global level.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by tree comparison analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Thirteen pairs of sister clusters with similar TF profiles were separated in the effector gene-based classification (divergent pattern).
claims.source: On the other hand, in glutamatergic/GABAergic neuronal classification, we surprisingly found that 13 pairs of sister clusters with similar TF profiles were separated in the effector gene-based classification.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: The population-level statistical analysis identified divergent pairs (n = 15) that were largely overlapped with those identified by hierarchical sister analysis (n = 10).
claims.source: Also, the population-level statistical analysis identified divergent pairs (n = 15, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) that were largely overlapped with those identified by hierarchical sister analysis (n = 10, Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: Sub-tectal glutamatergic neurons (cluster 24) and hindbrain GABAergic neurons (cluster 17) shared similar TF profiles but expressed different effector gene profiles.
claims.source: For examples, sub-tectal glutamatergic neurons (cluster 24) and hindbrain GABAergic neurons (cluster 17) shared similar TF profiles id2a/pax2a/zfhx4/meis1b, but expressed different effector gene profiles, cpne4a/c1ql4b/slc5a7a and gad1b/slc6a1b/slc6a5, respectively (Figure 3F)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as an example of divergent pattern and shown in violin plots in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Forebrain glutamatergic neurons (Cluster 30) and tectal GABAergic neurons (Cluster 11) shared TF profiles but had differentially expressed effector gene profiles.
claims.source: forebrain glutamatergic neurons (Cluster 30) and tectal GABAergic neurons (Cluster 11) shared TF profiles, bhlhe41/bcl11ba/mef2cb, but had differentially expressed effector gene profiles, adcyap1b/syt5b/rprml/gadd45bb, and kcnip1b/cxcl4/plxdc1, respectively (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as an example of divergent pattern and shown in violin plots in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Analysis of 3,883 sorted tectal glutamatergic neurons yielded 11 clusters.
claims.source: Analysis of 3, 883 sorted tectal glutamatergic neurons yielded 11 clusters (n = 11, Figure 4A), more than those identified from the whole-brain samples (n = 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the t-SNE plot in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The majority of tectal glutamatergic clusters (10/11) were stable using mean/median Jaccard index >0.6 as cutoff.
claims.source: The majority of clusters (10/11) were stable using mean/median Jaccard index >0.6 as cutoff (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the JaccardRainCloudPlot in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: A total of 574 tectal neurons were reconstructed from 263 zebrafish.
claims.source: Furthermore, using confocal imaging, we reconstructed a total of 574 tectal neurons (from 263 zebrafish, Figure 4—source data 2) that expressed one of these six TFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text describing the morphological analysis of tectal neurons.

claims.claim: Tectal neurons were categorized into seven morphological subclasses: bi-stratified (n = 36), mono-stratified (n = 71), non-stratified (n = 318), necklace-like (n = 76), cross-hemispheric (n = 15), ascending (n = 18), and descending (n = 40).
claims.source: These neurons were categorized into seven morphological subclasses: bi-stratified (I, n = 36), mono-stratified (II, n = 71), non-stratified (III, n = 318), necklace-like (IV, n = 76), cross-hemispheric (V, n = 15), ascending (VI, n = 18), and descending (VII, n = 40) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in representative images in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: All six TFs marked multiple morphological subclasses in a combinatorial manner, while each of seven morphological subclasses was marked by numerous TFs.
claims.source: Remarkably, all six TFs marked multiple morphological subclasses in a combinatorial manner, while each of seven morphological subclasses was marked by numerous TFs (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the matrix in Figure 4E displaying the expression of six TFs in seven morphological subclasses.

claims.claim: GO analysis of differentially expressed genes between sister clusters with divergent pattern showed that many genes encoded RBPs.
claims.source: We then performed GO analysis of differentially expressed genes between sister clusters of 10 pairs with different terminal features but similar TF profiles ('divergent pattern'). We surprisingly found that many differentially expressed genes encoded RBPs (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the dot plot in Figure 5A highlighting the category of post-transcriptional regulators.

claims.claim: Two forebrain glutamatergic neuronal clusters (Clusters 7 and 38) shared similar TF profiles but had different effector gene profiles and RBPs.
claims.source: Here were two examples: two forebrain glutamatergic neuronal clusters (Clusters 7 and 38) shared the similar expression pattern of TF profiles eomesa/neurod1/tbr1b/foxg1a, but had different effector gene profiles and RBPs, rprma/stxbp1b/egfl6/khdrbs2/msi2b/rbm5 and nrgna/susp5/fam43b/qkia/larp6a, respectively
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as an example of divergent pattern with differential RBP expression, shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: GABAergic neurons in hindbrain (Cluster 12) and sub-tectal (Cluster 16) shared TF profiles but differentially expressed effector genes and RBPs.
claims.source: GABAergic neurons in hindbrain (Cluster 12) and sub-tectal (Cluster 16) shared TF profiles, otpa/bhlhe41/id2a, but differentially expressed effector genes and RBPs, kctd4/rgs5b/cpne2/eif5a2/celf3a and slc6a1b/cplx2l /ndrg2/msi2b/rbfox1/msi2a, respectively (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as an example of divergent pattern with differential RBP expression, shown in violin plots in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: RBP-encoded genes exhibited wide RNA functions, including capping, splicing, polyadenylation, transport, stability, and translation.
claims.source: These RBP-encoded genes exhibited wide RNA functions, including capping, splicing, polyadenylation, transport, stability, and translation (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the 3D pie plot in Figure 5C displaying functional annotation of RBP genes.

claims.claim: The number of RBPs that were specific to divergent pattern (n = 52 from 10 pairs) was much more than those specific to either matched pattern (n = 7 from one pair) or convergent pattern (n = 10 from seven pairs).
claims.source: Also, we found that the number of RBPs that were specific to divergent pattern (n = 52 from 10 pairs) was much more than those specific to either matched pattern (n = 7 from one pair) or convergent pattern (n = 10 from seven pairs, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F.

claims.claim: In terms of the number of pattern-specific RBPs per pair, RBPs showed preferential expressions in divergent pairs compared to convergent ones.
claims.source: Thus, in terms of the number of pattern-specific RBPs per pair, RBPs showed the preferential expressions in divergent pairs compared to convergent ones (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the bar plot in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Divergent pattern-specific RBPs targeted significantly higher proportions of effector genes than matched and convergent pattern-specific RBPs.
claims.source: More importantly, divergent pattern-specific RBPs targeted significantly higher proportions of effector genes than matched and convergent pattern-specific RBPs (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the bar plot in Figure 5E displaying effector binding target proportion of pattern-specific RBPs.

claims.claim: Rbfox1-encoded gene was differentially expressed in multiple neuronal clusters.
claims.source: Interestingly, genes encoding well-known sequence-specific RBP Rbfox1-encoded gene was differentially expressed in multiple neuronal clusters, like 23/25, 27/54, 11/30, 13/24, 12/16, 2/3, and 7/38 (Figure 5—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5—source data 5.

claims.claim: Single RBPs were frequently present in multiple pair clusters (42.5%, 51/120).
claims.source: Moreover, we calculated the frequency of individual RBPs in marking all sister pair clusters with each of three patterns and found that single RBPs were frequently present in multiple pair clusters (42.5%, 51/120, Figure 5F), indicating that clusters mostly used RBPs in a combinatorial manner.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the bar plot in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The study analyzed approximately 65,000 single cells from the whole-brain, specific brain regions, neurotransmitter/neuromodulator-defined neuronal populations of the 8 dpf larval zebrafish.
claims.source: This study analyzed ~65,000 single cells from the whole-brain, specific brain regions, neurotransmitter/neuromodulator-defined neuronal populations of the 8 dpf larval zebrafish (Figures 1A, 2B ,, 4A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section summarizing the scope of the study.

claims.claim: The transcriptome analysis offered a close-to-full coverage of all cells (~100,000) in the zebrafish brain.
claims.source: Notably, our transcriptome analysis offered a close-to-full coverage of all cells (~100,000) in the zebrafish brain, providing multidimensional landscapes of TFs and post-transcriptional regulators in vertebrate whole-brain neuron classification (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section, comparing the number of cells analyzed (~65,000) to the total number of cells in the zebrafish brain (~100,000).

claims.claim: Sister pair clusters represent the finest molecularly defined neuronal subclasses based on effector gene profiles.
claims.source: These sister pair clusters represent the finest molecularly defined neuronal subclasses based on effector gene profiles.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section explaining the significance of analyzing sister clusters at hierarchical termini.

claims.claim: Phenotypic convergence is highly conserved from invertebrates to vertebrates.
claims.source: Combined with earlier findings of extensive phenotypic convergence of distinct neuron types in worms and flies (Gendrel et al., 2016; Konstantinides et al., 2018; Hobert and Kratsios, 2019), our findings in zebrafish strongly suggest that phenotypic convergence is highly conserved from invertebrates to vertebrates.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn by comparing the findings in zebrafish with previous studies in C. elegans and Drosophila cited in the text (Gendrel et al., 2016; Konstantinides et al., 2018; Hobert and Kratsios, 2019).

claims.claim: Combinatorial TFs and post-transcriptional regulators could work in concert to determine neuronal types in the larval zebrafish brain.
claims.source: Together, our findings suggest that combinatorial TFs and post-transcriptional regulators could work in concert to determine neuronal types in the larval zebrafish brain (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated in the discussion section and illustrated in the summary figure (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Neurons with similar transcriptomic phenotypes could arise from two different brain regions through different TF programs.
claims.source: Putting this finding into the context of neuron-type evolution, it raises the possibility that different brain regions independently give rise to similar neurotransmitter phenotypes through different TF programs.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion section based on the observation that similar pair clusters can come from different brain regions.

claims.claim: The 68 cell subclasses identified for the larval zebrafish (8 dpf) were confirmed in another fish brain of the same age and were largely recapitulated by cell subclasses identified from the juvenile zebrafish (23–25 dpf).
claims.source: In this study, the 68 cell subclasses that we have identified for the larval zebrafish (8 dpf) were confirmed in another fish brain of the same age and were largely recapitulated by cell subclasses identified from the juvenile zebrafish (23–25 dpf, Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F; Raj et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by NNLS analysis results shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, citing Raj et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Transcriptome-defined subclasses in the study largely represent stable neuronal subclasses.
claims.source: Thus, transcriptome-defined subclasses in our study indeed largely represent stable neuronal subclasses.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn in the discussion section based on the reproducibility of clusters across replicates and developmental stages, as well as morphological validation.

claims.claim: Distinct TFs can determine neuronal types with similar neurotransmitter identities in C. elegans, arguing for phenotypic convergence.
claims.source: Interestingly, distinct TFs can determine neuronal types with similar neurotransmitter identities in the Caenorhabditis elegans, arguing for phenotypic convergence (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013; Gendrel et al., 2016; Hobert and Kratsios, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cites three references (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013; Gendrel et al., 2016; Hobert and Kratsios, 2019) supporting the concept of phenotypic convergence in C. elegans.

claims.claim: Phenotypic convergence has been reported in Drosophila's optic lobe.
claims.source: Remarkably, this phenotypic convergence has also been reported in the Drosophila's optic lobe (Konstantinides et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cites Konstantinides et al., 2018 as evidence for phenotypic convergence in Drosophila.

claims.claim: Previous scRNA analysis of the zebrafish nervous system has demonstrated the temporal dynamics of brain cell development.
claims.source: Previous scRNA analysis of the zebrafish nervous system has elegantly demonstrated the temporal dynamics of brain cell development (Raj et al., 2018; Raj et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cites two references (Raj et al., 2018; Raj et al., 2020) describing previous zebrafish scRNA-seq studies.

claims.claim: Rbfox1 is an activity-dependent splicing regulator important in the transition from neuroprogenitors to neurons and in interneuron subtype-specific splicing in the mouse cortex.
claims.source: Previous studies have elegantly revealed the importance of activity-dependent splicing regulator Rbfox1 in the transition from neuroprogenitors to neurons as well as in the interneuron subtype-specific splicing in the mouse cortex (Zhang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and cites Zhang et al., 2016 as the source for the functional characterization of Rbfox1.

claims.claim: Rbfox1 specifically recognizes UGCAUG motifs, which are often found at 5′- and 3′-regions of introns.
claims.source: Rbfox1 specifically recognizes UGCAUG motifs, which are often found at 5′- and 3′-regions of introns (Yui Jin, 2003; Vuong et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and cites two references (Yui Jin, 2003; Vuong et al., 2018) describing the sequence specificity of Rbfox1.

claims.claim: Individual neuronal types could be well characterized by their transcriptomes.
claims.source: These studies have provided compelling evidence that individual neuronal types could be well characterized by their transcriptomes (Poulin et al., 2016; Tasic et al., 2018; Sugino et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cites three references (Poulin et al., 2016; Tasic et al., 2018; Sugino et al., 2019) supporting the use of transcriptomes to characterize neuronal types.

claims.claim: scRNA-seq analyses of half a million cells from the mouse brain showed that neurons could be classified by genes related to neuronal connectivity, synaptic transmission, and membrane conductance.
claims.source: For instance, scRNA-seq analyses of half a million cells from the mouse brain showed that neurons could be classified by genes related to neuronal connectivity, synaptic transmission, and membrane conductance (Zeisel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cites Zeisel et al., 2018 as the source for this finding in mouse brain.

claims.claim: The scRNA-seq analysis of nearly 200 genetically marked mouse neuronal populations showed that neurons could be classified by the expression level of various transcription factors, ion channels, synaptic proteins, and cell adhesion molecules.
claims.source: Besides, the scRNA-seq analysis of nearly 200 genetically marked mouse neuronal populations also showed that neurons could be classified by the expression level of various transcription factors (TFs), ion channels, synaptic proteins, and cell adhesion molecules (Sugino et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cites Sugino et al., 2019 as the source for this finding in mouse neuronal populations.

claims.claim: Regulatory genes encode proteins involved in gene transcription and translation (e.g., TFs and post-transcriptional regulators).
claims.source: Regulatory genes encode proteins involved in gene transcription and translation (e.g., TFs and post-transcriptional regulators), while effector genes encode proteins serving specific neuronal terminal features (e.g., synaptic proteins, ion channels, transporters, and receptors) (Kratsios et al., 2015; Zeisel et al., 2015; Paul et al., 2017, Zeisel et al., 2018; Reilly et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This definition is stated in the introduction and cites five references (Kratsios et al., 2015; Zeisel et al., 2015; Paul et al., 2017, Zeisel et al., 2018; Reilly et al., 2020) supporting this classification.

claims.claim: Regulatory genes are critical for establishing and maintaining effector gene profiles that resulted in diverse neuronal types.
claims.source: Regulatory genes are critical for establishing and maintaining effector gene profiles that resulted in diverse neuronal types.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a general principle of gene regulation in neuronal diversification.

claims.claim: Neuronal types could be well characterized by their features, including electrophysiological properties, neurotransmitter/modulator identity, synaptic connectivity, brain region identity, and cellular morphology.
claims.source: Previous studies have indicated that neuronal types could be well characterized by their features, including electrophysiological properties, neurotransmitter/modulator identity, synaptic connectivity, brain region identity, and cellular morphology (Zeisel et al., 2015; Pandey et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cites three references (Zeisel et al., 2015; Pandey et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018) supporting these criteria for neuronal classification.

results.result: The study generated single-cell transcriptomes from approximately 65,000-67,000 cells from 8 dpf larval zebrafish brains, representing close-to-full coverage of the ~100,000 total brain cells. Cells were obtained from whole brain and specific brain regions, then aggregated into 68 clusters using 1,402 high-variance genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8, C9, C10, C55, and C56 collectively establish the scope and coverage of the dataset. The numbers are internally consistent (65,253 cells obtained, 45,746 after filtering, ~67,000 reported in abstract), and the claim of near-complete coverage is reasonable given ~65,000 cells analyzed from ~100,000 total brain cells. The clustering methodology is clearly described.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering based on effector gene profiles (78.4% of variable genes, n=1,099) distinguished major brain cell types, segregating 68 clusters into neuronal (48 clusters, 37,880 cells) and non-neuronal (20 clusters, 7,866 cells) groups. Sister clusters at hierarchical termini displayed similar terminal features.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C17, C18, and C19 describe the hierarchical classification approach and its results. The methodology is well-documented with specific gene counts and cell numbers. The finding that effector genes dominate the variable gene set (78.4%) supports their use for classification. Bootstrap resampling with pvclust validates the hierarchical structure.

results.result: Most clusters demonstrated robustness with Jaccard index >0.6, including whole-brain clusters (most of 68), neuromodulator clusters (20/22), and tectal glutamatergic clusters (10/11).
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C22, and C42 consistently report cluster stability using Jaccard index analysis with a 0.6 cutoff threshold. The method is properly cited (Tang et al., 2020) and applied consistently across different datasets. The identification of specific unstable clusters adds credibility to the analysis.

results.result: Brain region-specific marker genes (foxg1a for forebrain, en2a for optic tectum, hoxb3a for hindbrain) were identified and showed conserved expression patterns in mouse brain. The ratio of glutamatergic to GABAergic neurons was highest in forebrain and lowest in hindbrain.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, and C14 describe regional marker identification and validation. The region-specific expression is shown in Figure 1D, and conservation in mouse is supported by three citations. The neurotransmitter distribution pattern is validated by transgenic fish imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).

results.result: The 68 cell clusters from 8 dpf larval zebrafish exhibited high overlap with juvenile zebrafish (23-25 dpf) brain clusters and were reproducible across biological replicates, indicating that transcriptome-defined subclasses represent stable neuronal subclasses.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C16, C61, and C62 establish developmental stability of identified clusters. NNLS analysis comparing with published juvenile data (Raj et al., 2018) is appropriate. Reproducibility across replicates and developmental stages, combined with morphological validation, supports the conclusion of stable subclasses.

results.result: Using Tg(ETvmat2:GFP) transgenic fish, 5,368 vmat2-expressing cells were obtained and aggregated into 22 neuromodulator clusters. The majority of 5-HT (8/14) and DA clusters (5/7) co-expressed GABAergic markers gad1b/gad2.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C21, and C23 describe neuromodulator neuron characterization. The transgenic approach is properly cited (Wen et al., 2008), cell numbers are specific, and the co-expression pattern is validated by dual transgenic imaging (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). The finding is consistent with previous studies (Filippi et al., 2014).

results.result: Glutamatergic/GABAergic sister clusters with similar effector gene profiles mostly expressed distinct TF profiles (convergent pattern: 7/8 pairs by intersection analysis). Examples include tectal and hindbrain glutamatergic clusters (1/31) and forebrain and sub-OT GABAergic clusters (36/16) sharing effector genes but expressing different TFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C29, C30, C31, and C35 establish the convergent pattern in neurotransmitter neurons. The analysis uses two complementary approaches (hierarchical and population-level) with intersection to increase confidence. Specific examples with gene names are provided. Subsampling validation (80% genes, 20 iterations) confirms robustness. The tree distance metric (0.71) quantitatively supports the distinction between TF and effector-based classifications.

results.result: Neuromodulator-type sister clusters predominantly expressed the same TF profiles (matched pattern: 5/6 pairs by intersection analysis). The tree distance between TF-based and effector-based hierarchies for neuromodulator neurons (0.38) was lower than for glutamatergic/GABAergic neurons (0.71).
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C32, C33, C34, C35, and C36 establish the matched pattern in neuromodulator neurons. The analysis methodology parallels that for neurotransmitter neurons, allowing valid comparison. The tree distance metric provides quantitative support for the qualitative observation. The statistical comparison (Fisher's exact test, p=0.02564) in C35 supports the differential pattern between neurotransmitter and neuromodulator types.

results.result: Glutamatergic/GABAergic clusters with similar TF profiles could display different terminal features (divergent pattern: 10 pairs by intersection analysis). Examples include sub-tectal glutamatergic and hindbrain GABAergic neurons (24/17) and forebrain glutamatergic and tectal GABAergic neurons (30/11) sharing TF profiles but expressing different effector genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C37, C38, C39, and C40 establish the divergent pattern. The methodology is consistent with convergent pattern analysis. The identification of 10 overlapping pairs between hierarchical (13 pairs) and population-level (15 pairs) analyses increases confidence. Specific examples with gene names are provided, including cases where paired clusters express different neurotransmitters, which is particularly striking.

results.result: GO analysis of differentially expressed genes between divergent pattern clusters revealed enrichment for RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). Divergent pattern-specific RBPs (n=52 from 10 pairs) were more numerous per pair than matched (n=7 from 1 pair) or convergent (n=10 from 7 pairs) pattern-specific RBPs, and targeted significantly higher proportions of effector genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C46-C52 establish the role of RBPs in divergent pattern clusters. GO analysis appropriately identifies RBP enrichment. The quantitative comparison of RBP numbers per pair across patterns is valid. The oRNAment database analysis linking RBPs to effector gene targets provides mechanistic support. However, the causality between RBP expression and effector gene divergence remains correlative rather than experimentally demonstrated.

results.result: Rbfox1 was differentially expressed in multiple neuronal cluster pairs, and single RBPs were frequently present in multiple pair clusters (42.5%, 51/120), indicating combinatorial use of RBPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C53 and C54 describe RBP usage patterns. The identification of Rbfox1 in multiple pairs is data-supported. The frequency calculation (42.5%) is specific and indicates combinatorial logic. This is consistent with known biology of post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: Analysis of 3,883 sorted tectal glutamatergic neurons yielded 11 clusters. Morphological reconstruction of 574 tectal neurons from 263 zebrafish identified seven morphological subclasses. All six examined TFs marked multiple morphological subclasses in a combinatorial manner, and each morphological subclass was marked by multiple TFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C43, C44, and C45 describe the tectal neuron morphology analysis. The experimental approach using BAC recombination and intersectional genetics is well-designed. Sample sizes are substantial (574 neurons from 263 fish). The finding of combinatorial TF-morphology relationships is clearly demonstrated in Figure 4E. However, the correlation between transcriptomic clusters and morphological subclasses is only partial (6/11 clusters, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), suggesting additional complexity.

results.result: TF-based and effector gene-based hierarchical trees were distinct (tree distance=0.71, only one matching node: Clusters 9/61). Of 11 effector gene-based sister clusters, only one pair matched in TF-based classification (matched pattern), while 10 were separated (convergent pattern). Population-level analysis identified 19 similar pairs: 5 matched and 14 convergent.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 provide methodological details supporting the convergent pattern finding. The TreeDist package provides quantitative tree comparison. The discrepancy between hierarchical (11 pairs) and population-level (19 pairs) analyses is acknowledged and addressed by intersection. The tree distance metric validates the qualitative observation of different organizational principles.

results.result: Phenotypic convergence (similar terminal features from different TF programs) is highly conserved from invertebrates to vertebrates, as similar patterns have been reported in C. elegans and Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C63, and C64 place findings in evolutionary context. The citations to C. elegans (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013; Gendrel et al., 2016; Hobert and Kratsios, 2019) and Drosophila (Konstantinides et al., 2018) work are appropriate. However, this is primarily a comparative/interpretive claim rather than a direct experimental result from this study.

results.result: Combinatorial transcription factors and post-transcriptional regulators work in concert to determine neuronal types in the larval zebrafish brain.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 represents the main integrative conclusion. It is supported by the convergent pattern (different TFs → similar effectors), matched pattern (same TFs → similar effectors), and divergent pattern (same TFs + different RBPs → different effectors) findings. However, the 'work in concert' phrasing implies functional interaction that is inferred from correlation rather than experimentally demonstrated through perturbation studies.

results.result: Sister pair clusters represent the finest molecularly defined neuronal subclasses based on effector gene profiles.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is a definitional/interpretive statement about the hierarchical analysis approach. It is logically supported by the methodology: sister clusters at hierarchical termini are by definition the most similar pairs in the effector gene-based classification. This provides justification for focusing analysis on these pairs.

results.result: Neurons with similar transcriptomic phenotypes could arise from two different brain regions through different TF programs.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is explicitly labeled as speculative in the evidence ('raises the possibility'). While the observation that similar pair clusters can come from different brain regions is data-supported, the evolutionary interpretation about independent origins versus divergence from common ancestors is not directly testable with the current data. This represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: The study builds on established knowledge about neuronal classification by transcriptomes, the definitions of regulatory versus effector genes, and previous zebrafish scRNA-seq studies demonstrating temporal dynamics of brain development.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C74 represent background knowledge and literature context. All claims are properly cited with appropriate references. These establish the conceptual framework for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear accurate based on the stated content.
